text: Linear regression is the oldest and most useful starting point in machine learning. It predicts a number — a price, a demand forecast, a delivery time — by drawing the best straight line through your data. It's simple enough to explain to anyone, fast to train, and it teaches ideas you'll reuse for the rest of the course: parameters, loss, and fit.

With one input feature, the model is simply a line — price equals intercept plus slope times square feet. The intercept is the predicted value when the feature is zero; the slope is how much the prediction changes for each extra unit. Training means choosing the intercept and slope, the model's parameters.

For any candidate line, each point has a residual — the gap between the actual value and the line's prediction. Ordinary least squares picks the intercept and slope that minimize the sum of squared residuals. That's exactly the mean squared error loss from Lesson 6, and for a line it can be solved directly with algebra — no iteration required.

Generating 60 illustrative houses where the true relationship is about $50,000 plus $120 per square foot, with noise added: fitting LinearRegression recovers an intercept of 45,825 and a slope of 119.5 — close to the true 50,000 and 120, with noise stopping an exact match, which is completely normal.

scikit-learn expects X as a two-dimensional array, which is why we call reshape negative 1, 1. The model predicts about $225,011 for a 1,500 square foot house. Every trained sklearn model exposes learned values with a trailing underscore — intercept_ and coef_.

Plotting the data as a scatter and the model as a line shows exactly what the fit looks like. Always plot when you can — a picture reveals curves, outliers, and clusters that a single score hides entirely.

model.score returns R-squared, the share of variation in price the line explains — 0.949 means the line explains about 95 percent of the variation here. Be careful, though — this was computed on the same data used for training. Real evaluation happens on a held-out test set, as in Lesson 7.

Four assumptions to keep in mind. Linearity — the relationship really is roughly a straight line, or you need squared terms or a different model. Independent errors — residuals aren't patterned or connected to each other. Roughly constant spread — errors stay about the same size across the range. And sensitivity to outliers — squaring residuals means one extreme point can tilt the whole line.

To recap: linear regression finds the intercept and slope that minimize squared residuals. In scikit-learn, that's LinearRegression dot fit, with intercept_ and coef_ telling you what was learned. R-squared summarizes fit, but only test data tells you how it generalizes. Next, we extend the line to many features at once with multiple regression.
